title: Latent Hotspot Atlas and Stage Ruleset - E2E Latency Tracing
body:
High-level summary:

This is a working notebook describing a small, targeted investigation into repeated end-to-end latency hotspots we see in production traces. Goal: build an "atlas" of persistent pathologies and a compact "stage ruleset" engineers can run to triage a trace quickly (and to automate checks in observability pipelines).

Why this doc exists (context):
- Multiple incidents last quarter where p99 spikes were persistent after an infra patch. Symptoms looked similar but root causes differed (kernel contention vs. KV cache miss storms vs. oversized microbatches).
- We need a short checklist + annotated examples so on-call or a new engineer can map a trace to a likely remediation without sifting raw spans for 30min.

Data & workload used:
- Production-sampled traces (random 1% ingestion) + focused captures during a controlled synthetic ramp.
- Workload: medium chat completions (avg seqlen: 512 tokens), histogram has long tail to 4096; frequent multi-turn contexts (prefixes common).
- Hardware: A100x2 nodes in pool-3; also repro on V100 nodes in staging.

Collection method / instrumentation notes:
- Traces collected via roadside agent (span points): request-recv -> tokenize -> model-load-check -> kv-read -> batch-wait -> attention-kernel -> kv-write -> decode-emit -> postprocess -> egress-send.
- Added microsecond-resolution timers at kernel entry/exit for attention and softmax kernels (via nvtx wrappers) during the controlled window.
- Sampling cadence: default 1% + 100% for any request hitting p95+.

Cohort definitions used for slicing:
- Short: seqlen <= 128
- Medium: 129..1024
- Long: >1024
- Cold: first request on a model replica in 600s since last served request
- Saturated: node GPU utilization > 85% at sample time

Representative quantiles (baseline aggregated over 24h capture):
- Overall: p50 48ms, p95 190ms, p99 880ms
- Short: p50 35ms, p95 120ms, p99 360ms
- Medium: p50 62ms, p95 230ms, p99 940ms
- Long: p50 210ms, p95 660ms, p99 2.8s
- Cold (across lengths): p99 shifts +40% vs warmed
- Saturated: p95/99 skew strongly (p99 ~3–4x baseline depending on batch mix)

Stage contribution synthesis (percent of end-to-end median for medium cohort, median numbers):
- Tokenize + preprocess: 3–5% (1.5–3ms)
- KV read (cache hit path): 8–12% (5–9ms)
- Batch wait (coalescing): 6–20% (varies; microburst sensitive)
- Attention kernel: 55–70% (dominant; 30–120ms depending on seqlen)
- KV write / post-cache: 4–8%
- Decode/emit & postprocess: 7–12%
- Egress & network tail: 2–6% (higher for remote clients)

Notes: attention kernel dominates for medium+long seqlen; for short requests, batch-wait variance and KV read miss storms become comparable.

Observed hotspot phenotypes (atlas entries):
1) Kernel-entrance jitter (phenotype: micro-dropdowns inside attention span)
- Signature: per-trace NVTX entry/exit show attention kernel lat spikes in bursts across traces on same node; GPU counters show context-switch increases.
- Typical cohorts: saturated nodes with mixed long/short batches.
- Likely root: kernel scheduling contention or bad CUDA stream utilization after a scheduler update.
- Quick checks: compare per-span GPU occupancy / active-context metrics; look for co-located long traces.

2) KV cache cold-ring (phenotype: clustered KV misses causing upstream stalls)
- Signature: many traces from same model replica have elevated KV read lat and increased batch wait immediately following a window of replica changes (scaling events) or KV evictions.
- Typical cohorts: cold + medium length, ramp-ups after autoscale.
- Likely root: cache eviction + synchronous miss resolution hitting disk or remote KV service.
- Quick checks: kv-read p95 time series, eviction logs, warmup counters.

3) Batch-surge blocking (phenotype: a single oversized coalescing event delaying many short requests)
- Signature: long tail on batch-wait stage for short cohort; downstream attention kernel time normal but end-to-end elevated; batch size histogram shows one large batch that many traces waited on.
- Typical cohorts: high QPS of short requests multiplexed with occasional long requests.
- Likely root: batching logic allowing huge max_batch when a long request arrives, causing short requests to wait.
- Quick checks: batch size distribution around the spike; look for single batch with size >> median.

4) Egress-network microtails (phenotype: low compute but long egress percent)
- Signature: small attention time but egress latency huge; correlated to specific egress route or remote DC.
- Typical cohorts: short requests served by certain region/egress path.
- Likely root: network SNI issues or ephemeral routing congestion.
- Quick checks: per-route egress timings, client-region mappings.

Stitching ruleset (triage checklist to apply in priority order):
- If p99 > 1s: slice by seqlen. If long cohort dominates p99, mark "attention-dominant" and run kernel metrics check.
- If short cohort dominates p99: inspect batch-wait histogram. If single-batch anomalies present, label "batch-surge".
- If p99 rise correlates with recent scaling events or replica churn: run KV eviction/warmup checks; label "kv-cold-ring".
- If attention kernel shows per-instance correlated spikes across many traces: run GPU context-switch & NVTX sampling; label "kernel-entrance-jitter" and consider rollback of recent driver/kernel change.
- If compute is low but egress high: check egress route & client region; label "egress-microtail".

Actionable mitigations (short-term and medium-term):
- Short-term: set conservative max_batch cap for mixes with >20% short requests; enable early-fallback for oversized batches (route to dedicated lane); increase KV cache retention on heavy replicas during ramp windows.
- Medium-term: implement KV read async hedging for cache misses; add per-node kernel run-queue monitoring; add smart batch-splitter that heuristically splits long requests from short ones during high QPS.
- Long-term: persistent model-aware routing (pin long-seqlen heavy traffic to shards with capacity) and tighter kernel tuning (stream per-request isolation, tweak CUDA stream priorities).

Quick playbook for oncall (3–8 min triage):
1) Load trace -> slice by seqlen and cohort.
2) Look at stage waterfall: is attention kernel contributing >50% of p99? If yes -> kernel/seqlen path.
3) If batch-wait is top contributor for short cohort -> check batch hist and throttle policy.
4) If KV-read p95 elevated across many traces -> check eviction logs and recent scaling events.
5) If network/egress dominates -> open a network ticket and switch region if available.

Example annotated trace excerpts: (IDs are synthetic but representative)
- trace-20241107-001: medium seqlen, p99=1.12s. Breakdown: attention 780ms (70%), batch-wait 120ms (11%), kv-read 80ms (7%), others 140ms. Observed 1 oversized coalesce at t+12ms.
- trace-20241108-143: short seqlen, p99=420ms. Breakdown: batch-wait 260ms (62%), attention 80ms, egress 40ms. Correlated to single large batch id #b-77.
- trace-20241110-099: long seqlen, p99=2.9s. Attention kernel microspikes on NVTX logs; GPU context-switch rate up 3x baseline.

Planned follow-ups / experiments (owners):
- MESH-1: run 24h controlled test with pinned batch cap (owner: Marcus Lee, due: 2024-11-25).
- MESH-2: inject KV warmup prefetch during scale-up events for 48h (owner: Evelyn Tran, due: 2024-11-30).
- MESH-3: enable NVTX micro-sampling on two staging nodes for one week to catch kernel-entrance jitter (owner: Diego Alvarez, due: 2024-11-22).

Open questions (notes-to-self):
- Are there driver/OS patches rolled to pool-3 in the 72h window before the July incident that correlate to kernel-entrance jitter? (need infra change log).
- Can we compute a lightweight "trace fingerprint" to bucket traces automatically into atlas phenotypes? (build a model/heuristic).

Bottom line / decision points:
- Immediate: temporarily cap max_batch for mixed workloads; schedule KV warmup experiment during next traffic ramp.
- Engineering: invest in automated phenotype classification on ingested traces; add small observability runbook for kernel scheduling metrics.

Notes and links: see linked artifacts above for relevant PR and ticket. This doc is intentionally concise; expand into a Confluence page once experiments complete with reproducible scripts and graphs.
